sweep_summary: Ese Ejja (esee1248) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Vuillermet 2012 pp. 199-200. The single target-list item, Key & Wyma 1964 'Analyzing stress in Chama (Tacanan)' (Chapman College Research Bulletin 1(1): 28-37), is about Ese Ejja word stress but could not be obtained: no digitized copy exists on archive.org or Google Books, no DOI/OpenAlex/S2 record, and HathiTrust/WorldCat/Scholar/Chapman Digital Commons are could not be reached by automated download; it is known only second-hand (Vuillermet 2012:199 reports K&W 1964:28 called stress phonemic-but-partly-predictable; Rolle & Vuillermet 2016:208 quote K&W 1964:31 on alternating secondary stress). Priority medium: historically the source of the surveys' 'penult' coding, but superseded by Vuillermet 2012. Three first-hand/secondary sources already held by the project were read and all confirm the catalog's classification: Rolle & Vuillermet 2016 (pp. 196, 198, 208), Rolle 2013 (pp. 268-269) and Guillaume in press (pp. 8-9) — initial three-syllable window, no default syllable, position set by suffix class, root transitivity and syllable count. An official open copy of Vuillermet 2012 was not reachable (theses.fr document endpoint timed out, HAL tel-05248962 has no file, Lyon 2 server unreachable). Best new statement: Rolle & Vuillermet 2016 p. 196/198 — confirms, does not supersede.

new_statements.quote: In this paper, we argue that Ese'eja (Takanan; Bolivia/Peru) also demonstrates this rare type of window. We report on findings of a verbal accent study (Vuillermet 2012), which systematically documents the position of accent in a large number of inflected verbs, resulting in a corpus of nearly 2,000 verb forms. This corpus demonstrates a three syllable window, and reveals a complex but consistent system varying according to (1) stem syllable count, (2) root transitivity, and (3) the type of suffix added. Accent position cannot be accounted for by reference to purely phonological structure such as syllable count, the quantity of the syllable, the quality of the vowel, or the sonority of the onset. [p.198:] The position of primary accent is dependent on its morphosyntactic environment, and any notion of a 'default' accent is difficult to establish.
new_statements.citation: Rolle, Nicholas & Marine Vuillermet. 2016. Morphologically assigned accent and an initial three syllable window in Ese'eja. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 12(1): 195-215. DOI 10.5070/P7121040731.

new_statements.reading: Primary word accent is confined to the first three syllables of the prosodic word, but which of the three it lands on is set by morphology (suffix accent group, root transitivity, stem syllable count) plus iterative footing, not by any phonological default or syllable weight; nouns and verbs pattern differently. This is a first-hand statement (Vuillermet is the grammar's author) that confirms the catalog's 'lexical' (non-fixed, morphologically determined) coding with a word domain.

new_statements.relation_note: 196-215 as printed), not the CUP version of record, which is paywalled (DOI 10.1017/9781316683101.013). Against the catalog's Gordon-coded parity pattern (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable): primary on σ1 in even-count words, σ2 in odd-count words, alternating secondaries) the paper agrees that primary accent is confined to the initial three syllables and that there is alternating rhythm, but it explicitly denies that syllable count determines the position and gives minimal pairs that break the parity rule: 4-σ ba.ná-ka-he (σ2, Gordon predicts σ1) beside í.she.’a-he (σ1); 5-σ bé.sa-ka-na.he (σ1, Gordon predicts σ2) beside to.wá.a-na.he (σ2)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary accent per prosodic word, always on one of the first three syllables. Which of the three is set by morphology: tense/mood suffixes fall into four Suffix Accent Groups (SAGs 1 and 3 accent the stem ultima, SAGs 2 and 4 the stem penult), root transitivity and stem syllable count shift the result, then iterative footing (iambic under SAG 1, trochaic under SAGs 2/3/4) runs across the word and the leftmost foot carries primary accent. No phonological default and no weight sensitivity. Primary accent is realized with higher pitch and greater intensity ('primary stress').
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 208: 'Vuillermet (2012: 199) notes that secondary stresses can be echoed every other syllable from the primary prominence, ‘but it is not always audible’ in fluent speech. Additionally, in early work on Ese’eja prosody, Key and Wyma (1964: 31) observed a ‘[predictable] secondary stress [that] automatically falls on every other syllable in both directions from the primary stress’.' The authors' own analysis has iterative feet giving rhythmic (secondary) accents across the word.
new_statements.exceptions: When morphologically assigned accent falls outside the initial three-syllable window (e.g. /ishe’a-ká-me/), primary prominence surfaces on a rhythmically dependent position inside the window ('rhythmic repair', §4.4). Nouns and adjectives show the same initial 3-σ window but are subject to accent shifts from clitics (p. 208, citing Vuillermet 2012: 200-205). The SAG 1 cophonology yields a three-syllable window while SAGs 2/3/4 yield only a two-syllable window (p. 209).
new_statements.identity_note: Rolle & Vuillermet 2016 describe the Madidi variant of Ese'eja as spoken in the Bolivian community of Portachuelo Bajo (p. 196-197: three variants Madidi, Palmareal and Baawaja; data from Vuillermet's fieldwork with Madidi speakers, principal consultant Calixto Callaú Casirno). Key & Wyma 1964 and Key 1968 use the older name 'Chama' for the language; Shoemaker & Shoemaker use 'Essejja'/'Ese'ejja'. Key 1968's SIL record lists the subject language as Tacana [tna], so its Ese Ejja coverage is unverified.

readall_conflicts: The one work opened (Rolle & Vuillermet 2016/2018, first-hand data from Vuillermet's fieldwork) disagrees with the catalog's Gordon-coded record, which is a pure syllable-count pattern (primary on the first syllable of even-count words and the second of odd-count words, secondaries alternating). Rolle & Vuillermet keep the initial three-syllable window and the alternating rhythm but state that accent position 'cannot be accounted for by reference to purely phonological structure such as syllable count' and show same-length verbs with different primary positions depending on suffix accent group and root transitivity. Guillaume's Takanan overview (held by the project from the earlier search, not in this works list) sides with Rolle & Vuillermet: 'no default syllable is identifiable.. a range of complex factors must be taken into account'. The unobtained Key & Wyma 1964 (cited second-hand as 'predictable secondary stress.. every other syllable in both directions') is the likely origin of the count-based coding, but it could not be checked; Shoemaker & Shoemaker 1965/1967 and Key 1968 could not be opened either.

audit.recode_to: morphological (non-contrastive, weight-insensitive accent assigned by root + affix/clitic properties inside an initial three-syllable window; nominal default = head of rightmost trochee, i.e. penult for bare 2-4 syllable nouns; verbs by stem syllable count x transitivity x suffix accent group). Also correct the 'contra' paraphrase: the source does NOT say stress is 'lexical, learned word by word' — Vuillermet 2012:199 says 'It is not contrastive' and 2012:225 'verbal accent is completely regular when the four parameters.. are considered'; only two nouns (aná, bishé, p.202) and five verbs (R&V 2016:201 fn.6) are irregular. Gordon 2002's 'even-numbered from R' matches only the bare-noun default and Key & Wyma's alternating secondaries, not the system.

Accent position cannot be accounted for by reference to purely phonological structure such as syllable count, the quantity of the syllable, the quality of the vowel, or the sonority of the onset." p.198: "The position of primary accent is dependent on its morphosyntactic environment, and any notion of a 'default' accent is difficult to establish." p.208: "This initial 3-σ window is also found in the nominal and adjectival systems".
sources.note: Primary accent (high pitch + intensity) is confined to an initial three-syllable window of the prosodic word; its exact syllable is assigned morphologically by suffix accent groups, root transitivity and stem syllable count, with iterative trochaic/iambic footing and the leftmost foot taking primary accent; no phonological default. Confirms the catalog's 'lexical' (morphologically determined, not fixed-position) coding and the word domain.

sources.quote: p.8: "Takanan languages have complex and still poorly understood accentual systems. The function of these systems is to delimit the phonological/prosodic word; none are lexically/morphologically constrastive. ... In the stress systems that have been studied (i.e., Ese Ejja, Araona, and Tacana), stress falls on one of the first three syllables counting from the left edge." p.9: "Stress in Ese Ejja also regularly falls in the initial three-syllable window. However, unlike Tacana and Araona, no default syllable is identifiable and, at least in verbal words, a range of complex factors must be taken into account for predicting its position, including the number of syllables, the transitivity of the root, and the type of suffixes used (see Vuillermet 2012a: 98ff; chap. 5; Rolle & Vuillermet 2019: 200)."
sources.note: Secondary summary citing Vuillermet 2012 and Rolle & Vuillermet 2019: Ese Ejja stress in an initial three-syllable window, no identifiable default syllable, position governed by syllable count, root transitivity and suffix type. Consistent with the catalog's classification.

sources.quote: Single primary accent on one of the first three syllables, correlate high pitch; distinct noun vs verb patterns; placement from 'inherent accent of a word, accent assignment from affixes/clitics, part of speech, clash resolution, trochaic footing, directionality, window'. Nouns without inherent/assigned accent: trochees from the right edge, primary = rightmost accent inside an initial 3-syllable window (ké, dáki, bawícho, iñawéwa); a few nouns carry inherent (lexical) accent, e.g. bishé 'canoe'.
sources.note: Reanalysis of Vuillermet 2012's data: primary stress on one of the first three syllables; nouns get trochaic feet from the right edge with word stress on the rightmost accented syllable inside the initial 3-syllable window (surface penult for 2-4 syllable bare nouns), overridden by inherent and affix-assigned accents; verbs differ by suffix group. Confirms the catalog's non-fixed, morphology-driven coding.
